title: The Temple (1 Kings 8)
hook: the heaven of heavens can't contain God, yet he chooses to dwell

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon was offered anything, and asked for wisdom. Your line was an understanding heart. Where did you listen before deciding? Day four hundred eight.

Seven years of building. Cedar from Lebanon, stone cut at the quarry so no hammer is heard on the site, gold over the inner walls. Solomon has built a house for God in Jerusalem, on the hill above his father's city. Now comes the day of dedication. The priests carry the ark of the covenant, the same ark David danced before, into the innermost room, the Holy of Holies, and set it under the wings of the cherubim. They step back out. And then something happens that nobody planned: a cloud fills the house. So thick that the priests can't stand to do their work. The text says the glory of the Lord had filled the house.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS OF BUILDING.` → `THE ARK INTO THE HOLY OF HOLIES.` → `A CLOUD FILLS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Solomon stands before the altar in front of the whole assembly, spreads his hands toward heaven, and prays. And right in the middle of the proudest day of his reign, he says something that undercuts his own building. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is it then to be thought that God should indeed dwell upon earth? for if heaven, and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?" He knows. No building can hold God. The whole sky can't. So what is the Temple for? Solomon answers in the rest of the prayer: so that God's eyes may be open on this house night and day, and God will hear whoever prays toward it. The sick, the guilty, the soldier far away, even the foreigner who comes from a distant land. The Temple isn't a box for God. It's a place God chooses, freely, to be found. That's the line to hold: he can't be contained, and still he chooses to dwell. Catholics see that choice taken further. John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and Jesus calls his own body a temple. Saint Paul tells Christians they themselves are God's temple. And in Catholic churches there's a tabernacle, often with a lamp burning beside it, where the Blessed Sacrament is kept, because Catholics believe Christ is truly present there. People kneel or genuflect as they pass. Solomon's question still stands: can God really dwell on earth? The Catholic answer is yes: not because anyone built something big enough, but because, Catholics say, he chooses to.
screen: `CAN GOD DWELL UPON EARTH?` · `A PLACE WHERE GOD WILL HEAR.` · `THE WORD DWELT AMONG US.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND ITS LAMP.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS OF HEAVENS CANNOT CONTAIN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a small space holy. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are and pick one small spot: a corner of a shelf, a windowsill, the dashboard, a bedside table. Picture what could mark it as a place to stop. A candle, a cross, a picture of someone you love, a stone from a walk, an empty space kept clear on purpose. It doesn't need to be big. Solomon knew size wasn't the point. If you pray, you can ask God to meet you there. If you don't, let it be a place you come back to yourself. The bell holds the time.
The Temple. The house Solomon built in Jerusalem, filled with God's glory, which he knew could never contain God, a place God chose to be found. Today's word.
Your line: he chooses to dwell. Today, set aside your small space, and stop there once before the day is done. Day four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Catholic churches keep the Blessed Sacrament in a tabernacle, usually with a sanctuary lamp burning nearby, and Catholics genuflect toward it; the Church also keeps feasts for the dedication of churches, including the Lateran Basilica in Rome.

fork.setup: you're Solomon. you've spent seven years building the finest house in the land for God, and today you dedicate it before all Israel. what do you say?
options: now God lives here, with us.
even heaven can't contain you, how much less this house.
fork.reveal: at the height of his triumph, Solomon admits no building can hold God, and asks only that God hear the prayers made toward it.

original.note: Hebrew: house. The Temple is called the house of the Lord; the same word means a family, a dynasty, a home.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Temple was where God lived.
what it means: Solomon knew no house could hold God. the Temple was the place God chose to be found, and where prayers would be heard.
what a scholar hears: 2 Samuel 7 plays on bayit: David wants to build God a house, and God promises to build David a house, a dynasty, instead. Solomon's Temple sits where the two meet.

sources.quoted: Is it then to be thought that God should indeed dwell upon earth? for if heaven, and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?

notes: Seven years of building (1 Kings 6:38) and no hammer heard on site (6:7): confirm.
Solomon's prayer for the foreigner: 1 Kings 8:41–43; confirm.
'The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14) is spoken without quotation marks as a paraphrase, though it matches the Douay; confirm whether to cite as quoted.
CCC 1379 on the tabernacle and Real Presence; confirm the reference.
Trapdoor: the bayit wordplay in 2 Samuel 7 (Nathan's oracle) is standard; confirm.
